summary: This paper introduces circuit balancing and depolarizing parameter estimation techniques to mitigate two-qubit gate errors in unitary $k$-design circuits without two-qubit gate overhead. The method leverages the uniform Pauli support distribution of such circuits, combined with gate benchmarking data and Pauli twirling to suppress coherent error, achieving over 92% Hellinger distance reduction in simulations and doubling the Loschmidt echo survival probability on IBM Fez.
motivation: Existing error mitigation techniques like zero-noise extrapolation and tensor-network methods incur prohibitive circuit depth overhead or fail in high-entanglement regimes, limiting their applicability to deep, scrambling circuits that represent unitary $k$-designs relevant for simulating quantum chaos and other physical systems.
method: The authors exploit the fact that for balanced circuits (where each qubit pair undergoes similar total depolarization), the average per-gate depolarizing contribution to the global channel scales as $\lambda_2^{15/16}$. Circuit balancing is formulated as an optimization problem over qubit layout assignments. After benchmarking extracts gate-level depolarizing parameters $\lambda_2$, the global parameter $\lambda_n$ is estimated, Pauli twirls suppress coherent error with $t \geq O(m\theta^2\delta^{-2}\lambda^{-15/16 \cdot 2}_d)$ twirls required, and bitstring probabilities are inverted via $S^{-1}(\lambda_n, p_i)$ and projected onto the probability simplex.
result: Numerical experiments show $\geq 92\%$ mean Hellinger distance reduction across $n=7$–$11$ qubits, with stability under varying coherent error strengths ($\theta \in \{3, 6, 9\} \times 10^{-3}$ rad) when $t$ scales quadratically in $\theta$. On IBM Fez, balanced layout with inversion achieved $> 2 \times$ ground-state survival probability in Loschmidt echo ($\sim 0.3$ vs. $\sim 0.15$ unmitigated) with circuit balancing cost function $6.17 \times 10^{-5}$.
